## Exercise 2: Import tidy data
```{r}
# Import the data
survey <- read.csv("https://mac-stat.github.io/data/112_fall_2024_survey.csv")
```


## Exercise 3: Tidy data properties

Each row represent how students in mac eat a type of food, how long will it take them, the temperature they like, and the place they like
cafe_mac is a categorical variable, fave_temp is a quantitative variable.


## Exercise 4: Get to know the data

```{r}
# It shows the number of row and column in the dataset.
dim(survey)

# It shows the number of row of this dataset.
nrow(survey)

# It shows the first 6 rows of this dataset.
head(survey)

# It shows the first 3 rows of this dataset.
head(survey, 3)

# It shows the last 6 rows of this dataset.
tail(survey)

# It shows the name of the columns.
names(survey)
```


## Exercise 5: Data structure

```{r}
# Obtain the overall class of the survey object

sur <- survey
class(sur)



# Examine the structure of each variable within survey (including class)

cafe_mac <- "fried rice" 
class(cafe_mac)

minutes_to_campus <- 15
class(minutes_to_campus)

fave_temp <- 18.3
class(fave_temp)

hangout <- "a forest"
class(hangout)

## cafe_mac is character, minutes_to_campus is integer, fave_temp is numeric, hangout is character.

# Just take note of what information we gain here (no need to write more)
## We have the dimension of the dataset, the class of the variables, and first few columns of each variable.

```




## Exercise 6: Your turn

```{r}
# Import and name the dataset (you pick a name!)

football <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2022/2022-11-29/worldcups.csv")

# Print the first 6 rows of the dataset

head(football)

# How many years of data do we have? And how many measurements do we have on each year?

dim(football)

## There are 21 years and 10 measurements.

# Get a list of all variable names in the dataset

names(football)

# Display the class and other information for each variable in the dataset
str(football)
summary(football)

```
